<reason>Both sides argued well, but PRO built the broader and better-weighed case. CON's defense rested almost entirely on the high-earning tipped server's "upside," and PRO named that gap early and never let it go ("a case built on the lottery's winners is not a case for the lottery"), extending the comparison to the lunch server, the dead section, the accented server, and the kitchen — constituencies CON largely left unaddressed except by pointing to the statutory minimum-wage top-up. PRO's variance-allocation frame (the business that sets prices and schedules should carry the risk, not the worker with the thinnest cushion) gave a clean decision rule that CON never displaced. CON's best moves were real: the tip-as-worker-property point, service charge as house revenue, the Meyer reversal, the DC/Maine worker opposition, and above all the "disclosure vs. abolition — pick one" dilemma sharpened in closing. But PRO neutralized the two most dangerous: it turned owner discretion back on CON's own tip-pooling remedy (if owners can't be trusted with a service charge, they can't be trusted with a pool), and it answered the "statute invented in speech four" charge by pointing out that "higher base pay" is in the motion itself and base pay is already the strongest legal wage claim. PRO also converted CON's stacked concessions (legible menus, raise the floor, pool with the kitchen) into the observation that compensation would no longer *rely* on tipping — which tracks the motion's actual wording. CON's closing dilemma remains a live but narrower route, and PRO's repeated over-cap clipping is a genuine execution cost, which keeps this from being a solid win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's [A4.2] tu quoque — CON's kitchen remedy (tip pooling) depends on the same owner discretion CON claims is fatal to service charges — plus its answer that "higher base pay" is already in the motion, blunted CON's strongest structural attack that PRO's mechanism required a statute invented mid-debate.</best_rebuttal>
